parts.title: Reporting a broadband fault
parts.context: A customer phones an internet company about a connection problem.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a customer phoning an internet company to report a fault. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Good afternoon, Skyline Broadband, Callum speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: anita
script.text: Hello. My internet keeps dropping out, and it's making it impossible to work from home.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. I'll take some details and see what we can do.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller's connection keeps dropping out, so 'dropping' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Could I have your surname, please?

script.speaker: anita
script.text: It's Brightwell. That's B-R-I-G-H-T-W-E-L-L.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Thank you, Ms Brightwell. Can you look at your router for me? What colour is the light on the front?

script.speaker: anita
script.text: It was green, but today it's flashing red.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: That tells me the line has a fault. When did the problem start?

script.speaker: anita
script.text: On Monday evening. It was fine on Sunday, and I thought it would fix itself.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Have you tried anything yet?

script.speaker: anita
script.text: Yes, I've turned the router off and on again, and I've also reset it with a pin, but nothing changed.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Good. Does anyone else on your street have the same problem?

script.speaker: anita
script.text: I asked my neighbour, but she's with a different provider, and hers is working perfectly.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: In that case, I'd like to send an engineer. The earliest appointment is on the seventh of May.

script.speaker: anita
script.text: That's fine. What time would that be?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: It's a morning visit, between eight o'clock and twelve. The engineer will call you half an hour before.

script.speaker: anita
script.text: OK. Will I need to be at home?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Yes, an adult must be there. The engineer will need access to the loft, because that's where the cable comes into the house, so please make sure the way is clear.

script.speaker: anita
script.text: I'll move the boxes. Will there be a charge?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: If the fault is in our network, it's free. If it's in your own wiring, there's a charge of sixty pounds, but I don't think that's likely in your case.

script.speaker: anita
script.text: Understood. How will I know the appointment is confirmed?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: You'll get a text message in the next few minutes, and another one an hour before the engineer arrives.

script.speaker: anita
script.text: Great. Thank you for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A chocolate factory tour
parts.context: A guide explains the stages of chocolate making before a tour.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide introducing a tour of a chocolate factory. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: Welcome to Ashby's Chocolate Factory. I'm Julie Wright, and I'll be taking you round the production floor today. We follow the same route as the cocoa beans, so I'll tell you what happens in each area as we reach it.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: The first stop is the roasting hall. The beans are heated there for about thirty minutes, and the smell is wonderful. Roasting is what gives chocolate its flavour.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: Before roasting, in a separate room, the shells are removed from the beans, but we don't visit that room because it is very noisy and dusty.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: Next is the grinding room. Here the cleaned beans are crushed into a thick, dark paste, which is the base of all chocolate. It's bitter, so you wouldn't want to eat it as it is.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: In the mixing room, sugar is added, and for milk chocolate, milk powder as well. The mixture is then stirred and kneaded in huge machines, and this is the secret of our chocolate. The mixing goes on for up to three days, which is far longer than most other factories, and it makes our chocolate unusually smooth.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: Then the warm chocolate goes to the moulding hall, where it is poured into moulds to give it its shape. They cool in a long tunnel, and then they come out.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: And finally the packing area, where machines wrap the bars, and the boxes are sealed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: A few facts. The factory makes about fifty tonnes of chocolate every week, which sounds a lot, but it's small compared with the big companies. Our dark bars are the most popular, though the milk bars sell well in the shop.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: Some of you will have allergies. If you are allergic to nuts, please tell me before we go into the production area. I'll give you a green sticker, so that our staff know, and we keep nut products in a separate part of the building.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: At the end of the tour, you'll taste three pieces of chocolate, in the tasting room. You'll be asked to describe the flavour of each one, and there are no wrong answers.

script.speaker: wright
script.text: And if you like what you taste, you'll get twenty percent off in our shop if you show your ticket, but only today. Right. Please put on your hairnets, and follow me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A project on water filters
parts.context: Two engineering students write up the design and testing of a water filter.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two engineering students, Ali and Freya, discussing a project to build a water filter. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: Ali, shall we go through the design of the filter for the report? I'd like to describe it from the top to the bottom.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: Sure. The water goes into the tank at the top first. That's a plastic container, which holds about ten litres.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: Then it flows down through a layer of gravel, which stops the big particles, like leaves and stones.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: After that comes the sand. It's the main filter, and it traps the smaller particles. We used fine sand, which we washed first.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: Below the sand is a layer of charcoal, which removes the bad taste and smell. It doesn't remove bacteria, though, which is one limitation.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: And right at the bottom there's a piece of cloth, which catches any fine pieces of charcoal that might come through.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: That's the whole design. We should add a diagram, shouldn't we?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: Now the testing. How did we check the water quality?

script.speaker: freya
script.text: We used a testing kit from the laboratory. It measures cloudiness, which is the main thing, and acidity.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: The results were good. The dirty water was very cloudy, and after filtering it was almost clear.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: Yes, the cloudiness fell by about ninety percent. But it's important to say that cloudy water isn't necessarily unsafe, and clear water isn't necessarily safe.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: Right. So in the conclusion we should say that the filter improves the appearance and taste, but the water still has to be boiled before drinking.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: And how long did it take to filter a litre?

script.speaker: ali
script.text: About four minutes at the start, but it got slower with each use, as the sand clogged up.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: So in the recommendations, we should say that the sand needs to be replaced every month.

script.speaker: ali
script.text: Good point. Also, we ought to mention the cost. The whole filter cost less than five pounds to build.

script.speaker: freya
script.text: That's a strong selling point for villages without clean water. Shall I write that part?

script.speaker: ali
script.text: Please. And I'll draw the diagram tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of the postal service
parts.context: A lecture on how postal services developed, from Persia to postcodes.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of the postal service. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Sending messages over long distances has always mattered to governments, and so the postal service is one of the oldest public services in the world.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Early empires needed to control distant provinces. In ancient Persia, a network of roads allowed royal messengers to travel hundreds of kilometres, changing horses at stations along the way. The Romans later built their own system, called the cursus publicus, which was only for official messages. Ordinary people had to rely on friends or servants.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In Europe, the first services open to the public developed in the seventeenth century. Even then, the system was not what we know today. The recipient, not the sender, paid for the letter, and the price depended on the distance and the number of pages. People sometimes refused a letter, because they couldn't afford it.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: This was changed by a British teacher called Rowland Hill, who argued that a letter should cost the same, wherever in the country it was sent, and that the sender should pay in advance. His idea led to the world's first adhesive postage stamp, the Penny Black, in eighteen forty. It showed a portrait of Queen Victoria.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The result was dramatic. The number of letters sent more than doubled within a few years, because the cost fell so far.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Letters still had to cross borders, and each country had its own rules and charges. In eighteen seventy-four, an international agreement was signed in Bern, creating what became the Universal Postal Union, so that a letter could cross several countries with a single stamp.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One more innovation was the postcode, which sorts mail by location, so machines could read the address. In Britain, postcodes were fully introduced in the early nineteen seventies. Today, email has reduced the number of letters, but online shopping has created a boom in parcels. Next week we'll look at the history of the telephone.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
